extracted.intended_audience: press officers, science journalists, researchers of science communication, and scientists involved in producing/approving press releases
extracted.subtask_description: Content-analytic framework for assessing exaggeration, caveats, justifications, and advice in health- and biomedical-related press releases and the news derived from them, relative to the associated peer-reviewed journal article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advice to readers — four-level coding
rubrics_metrics.description: Each source was coded for maximum level of advice out of four possible categories: no advice, implicit advice, explicit advice but not to the reader or general public, or explicit advice to the reader or general public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: implicit advice — 'for adults with a BMI greater than 35 kg/m2…permanent calorie reductions of more than 500 calories per day would be needed…'; explicit but not to reader — 'clinicians must exercise caution in their use of aflibercept'; explicit to reader/general public — 'patients who are at increased risk of cardiovascular events should consider starting statin treatment promptly and continuing it long-term'. Include set of journal article, press release and news in analysis only if at least one source contained implicit or explicit advice. Caveats/justifications for advice are coded only where explicit advice appears.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causal claims — seven-level strength coding
rubrics_metrics.description: Press releases, news articles and journal articles were coded for the strength of the main statement of findings according to seven levels: no statement, statement of no relationship, correlational, ambiguous, conditional causal, can cause, and causal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coding applied to the title and the first two sentences of news and press releases, and the abstract and discussion in journal articles. Analysis focused on correlational cross-sectional and longitudinal designs; qualitative, intervention, or simulation designs were excluded for this causal-claim analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human inference from non-human research — three-category coding
rubrics_metrics.description: For journal articles based on non-human samples (animals, cells, or simulations), the associated press release and news article were coded as explicitly non-human, implicitly human, or explicitly human.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to detect message creep where non-human research is presented as applying to humans. Analysis may be limited by low N; report partial results when counts are too small for further analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveats — presence/absence for causal statements and for explicit advice
rubrics_metrics.description: Coded presence or absence of caveats for causal/correlational statements and coded caveats for explicit advice when such advice appeared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caveats are examples like 'We still need more research to clarify whether vitamin D directly prevents bowel cancer...' or justifications for strength of conclusions. Because caveats are rare, datasets may be combined (e.g., journal + university press releases) to analyse effects. Note typical placement (often at end of press releases) and that caveats are evaluated for whether they affect news uptake and whether they appear in resulting news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justifications — presence/absence for causal claims and advice
rubrics_metrics.description: Coded presence or absence of justifications (statements explaining why a conclusion is justified) for causal statements and for explicit advice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justifications for causal statements were coded if the press release contained any explicit statement of relationship; justifications for advice were coded only for those that contained explicit advice. Analyses examine whether justifications influence news uptake and whether they are transmitted into news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exaggeration (message creep) — operational definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Exaggeration was defined as claims or advice in press releases or news that were coded at a level above any of the associated statements in the peer-reviewed paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This treats the peer-reviewed journal article as the baseline; it does not attempt to judge whether the journal article itself is scientifically exaggerated. Examples: changing 'related to' or 'might increase' to 'boosts' would be coded as exaggeration if the journal article did not make such a causal claim. Exaggeration metrics include percentage of press releases/news with exaggeration and odds ratios for association between press release exaggeration and news exaggeration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Main-statement selection rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Main claims are assessed in the title and first two sentences of press releases and news, and in the abstract and discussion of the journal article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: first two sentences typically state the main claims and have largest influence on readers. This rule defines the text span used for coding advice level and causal-claim strength, rather than statements further down the article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion/exclusion criteria for causal-claim analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyses of causal claims focused on studies based on correlational cross-sectional and longitudinal designs; qualitative, intervention, or simulation designs were excluded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only press releases and articles describing relevant study designs were included in the causal-claims dataset; this restriction ensures comparability when coding correlational vs causal wording.

rubrics_metrics.name: News uptake metrics — binary and count measures
rubrics_metrics.description: News uptake measured as (a) whether a press release had at least one resulting news article (binary), and (b) the number of news stories per press release (count).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare press releases with and without particular features (exaggeration, caveats, justifications) using bootstrapped 95% confidence intervals and standard inferential tests. When multiple news articles arise from one press release, account for clustering in analyses of news-level outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coding protocol, instrument and reliability standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Data were recorded using a set list of questions (191 questions in the coding sheet). Double-coding was performed on a random subset to assess reliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 27.5% of press releases and 24.7% of news stories were double-coded yielding concordance of 98.3% (κ = 0.97). Where resources constrain choice between more double-coding or collecting more samples, increasing sample size may be statistically preferred when concordance is already high.

rubrics_metrics.name: Baseline assumption — use peer-reviewed paper as comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: The peer-reviewed journal article was always taken as the baseline against which press releases and news were compared to identify exaggeration (i.e., 'exaggeration beyond any that might already exist in the peer-reviewed paper').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This methodological choice avoids making subjective judgements about scientific accuracy of the journal article itself; authors note that if papers themselves contain exaggeration, total exacerbation rates measured this way will be underestimates.
